items.criterion: The recap's total runtime is between 120 and 150 seconds inclusive.
items.why: The brief specifies "two minutes to two-and-a-half" → 120-150 s. A 1:30 cut or a 3:00 cut violates the brief's runtime band. Source calibration: the golden NEON trailer runs 2:16.
items.check: Judge reads the recap's total duration from playback or container metadata visible in the player. Pass if 120 ≤ duration_seconds ≤ 150.

items.criterion: The recap is delivered as an mp4 file with 16:9 widescreen video and a stereo (or mono) audio track that plays without errors.
items.why: Theatrical/YouTube delivery convention; failure to deliver a playable 16:9 mp4 is a delivery failure regardless of editorial quality.
items.check: Judge confirms the file plays from start to end without skipping, that the frame is 16:9 (or pillarboxed to 16:9), and that audio is audible. Pass if all three hold.

items.criterion: A full-screen card containing the single word "PARASITE" appears anywhere in the final 25 seconds of the recap.
items.why: A late title card is the structural payoff of a teaser; landing the title early signals the wrong subtype (this would be a logo card, not a trailer climax). Source calibration: the golden trailer drops the PARASITE card at 02:07 of 02:17.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of a full-screen card whose largest visible text reads "PARASITE" (case-insensitive). Pass only if that timestamp is in the last 25 seconds of the recap's runtime.

items.criterion: No part of the recap is visibly stretched or squashed (faces noticeably wider or narrower than natural, circular objects rendered as ovals from anamorphic squeeze).
items.why: Aspect-ratio distortion is the most common silent delivery failure when an agent reframes 1.85:1 or 2.39:1 source into a different output container.
items.check: Judge inspects three sample frames (one near 10%, one near 50%, one near 90% of runtime) and confirms no visible horizontal/vertical stretch. Pass only if all three are undistorted.

items.criterion: Within the first 20 seconds of the recap, at least one shot establishes a cramped, dimly-lit, cluttered Korean semi-basement / low-ceilinged interior with at least one of its inhabitants visible at floor level or in tight framing.
items.why: The trailer's identity hinges on opening in the Kim family's poor-world before it ever shows the rich-world; this is what lets the genre shift later announce itself. Source calibration: the golden opens 00:00-00:16 with the stinkbug shot and the family huddled during fumigation in their semi-basement.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of a shot inside a cramped, low-light, working-class interior (boxes/clutter, low ceiling, no glass walls) where at least one human figure is present. Pass only if that timestamp is ≤ 20 seconds.

items.criterion: At least one shot in the recap shows the interior or grounds of a large modernist hillside house with high ceilings, exposed concrete or wood, large floor-to-ceiling glass walls, OR a manicured sunlit lawn.
items.why: The Park mansion is the visual antipode the trailer needs in order to make the class mirroring legible. A trailer that never leaves the poor-world has lost half the film. Source calibration: the golden devotes ~00:33-01:10 to the Park house interior and grounds.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of a shot whose visible space matches the modernist-mansion description (open glass, manicured outdoor space, designed minimalist interior). Pass if at least one such timestamp exists.

items.criterion: The recap contains at least one identifiable Act-1 con / heist beat from the film, recognisable without subtitles or VO: (a) someone Photoshopping or doctoring a document on a computer screen, (b) a young woman delivering a rehearsed-sounding rhythmic English-language self-introduction outside a residential gate ("Jessica" jingle), (c) someone visibly planting an article of clothing in a parked car, (d) a slow-motion or stylized shot of fuzz/peach-skin being blown into the air, or (e) multiple members of one family lounging on the furniture of a clearly different, wealthier household.
items.why: The film's first half is a con-comedy; the trailer cannot withhold the third act without keeping the heist spine legible. A teaser that omits all five of these beats has flattened the genre-shift the entire task is about. Source calibration: the golden uses (b) at 01:13-01:24, (a) at 00:27, (d) at 01:31, (e) at 01:34.
items.check: Judge cites at least one recap timestamp matching one of (a)-(e). Pass if a single one of the five visibly occurs and is dwelled on for ≥ 1 second of screen time.

items.criterion: Within the final 30 seconds of the recap (excluding any silent billing-block tail), there is an accelerated montage sequence that contains at least three distinct atmospheric shots drawn from this catalogue, with NO shots of physical violence between people: rain or water on glass; a child alone in a glowing tent or under a flashlight beam; a macro shot of red liquid (sauce / juice / paint) dripping or spreading; an extreme close-up of an adult face in tense thought; water rising or flowing on a domestic floor; hands or feet in low light without context.
items.why: The pre-title stinger montage is the convention by which a teaser implies a darker turn without spoiling it. The catalogue lists trailer-safe textures; the explicit exclusion of inter-person violence is the load-bearing constraint. Source calibration: the golden stings at 01:55-02:06 with pizza-sauce-as-blood, sewage flooding, Ki-taek's face, Da-song in the tent, never violence.
items.check: Judge cites three distinct recap timestamps within the final 30 seconds, each matching one entry in the catalogue, and confirms that none of those three shots depicts one human harming another. Pass only if at least three distinct catalogue entries are cited AND none of them is a violence shot.

items.criterion: The average shot length in the recap's final 30 seconds is visibly shorter than the average shot length in the recap's first 30 seconds.
items.why: Trailer-craft signature: the back-half cuts faster than the front-half to manufacture momentum into the title. A monotonous cut rate kills the curiosity arc the brief asks for.
items.check: Judge counts the number of distinct shots (hard cuts ignoring sub-frame dissolves) in the first 30 seconds (S_open) and in the final 30 seconds excluding any post-title billing tail (S_close), then computes whether S_close > S_open. Pass if S_close is strictly greater than S_open.

items.criterion: At least one shot in the final third of the recap shows a member of the Park household (an adult woman in upscale clothing, a husband-figure in business attire, a child of grade-school age, or a teen girl) showing visible unease, fear, suspicion, or shock, without depicting any act of violence happening to or by them.
items.why: The genre shift is announced through *faces*, not through the violence itself. This is the trailer's primary tool for telling the viewer "something is wrong" while still hiding what. Source calibration: golden ends on Mrs. Park's shocked face at the kitchen table at 02:14, and uses Da-song in his tent at 02:02 as a child-unease beat.
items.check: Judge cites a recap timestamp in the final third of runtime showing a person inside a clearly wealthy domestic space (high ceilings, glass walls, designer furniture) whose facial expression reads as fear/suspicion/shock, where no act of violence is visible in the same shot. Pass if at least one such timestamp exists.

items.criterion: The recap contains no continuous black-frame or solid-blank segment lasting 1.5 seconds or longer, other than a single distributor/billing-block tail card.
items.why: Black-frame padding is a common agent failure when output runtime is being padded to hit a target.
items.check: Judge scrubs through the recap and counts the longest continuous segment of solid black / blank frames outside any closing billing-block card. Pass if that longest segment is < 1.5 seconds.

items.criterion: No single shot from the recap is reused three or more times. (A shot reused twice for narrative parallelism is allowed; reuse three or more times is treated as padding.)
items.why: Repeated reuse of the same footage is the textbook agent failure when source coverage is thin or when output duration is being padded.
items.check: Judge identifies the most-repeated shot in the recap by visible content (same framing, same subject pose, same lighting) and counts its appearances. Pass if no shot appears 3+ times.

items.criterion: The recap does NOT contain any of: a person blinking a flashlight/lamp on-and-off as Morse code; on-screen text spelling out the film's ending or moral; a shot of a child or adult lying ill and recovering in a hospital; a contemplative "dream" or wish-fulfilment montage of someone buying or moving into the Park house.
items.why: The film's coda spells out the resolution; a teaser must end on a question. This absence item blocks the most common "explainer accidentally included" failure mode. Source calibration: these all live in the 02:04-02:12 region of the film.
items.check: Judge confirms none of the four named resolution images appears anywhere in the recap. Pass only if none are present.

items.criterion: The recap establishes a four-person family unit (one older man, one older woman, one young adult man, one young adult woman) who appear together or in adjacent shots, framed as a single family living in the same cramped lower-class home.
items.why: The trailer's narrative arm needs a protagonist family before it can be a heist trailer. A trailer that shows only one Kim member or splits the family into unrelated character introductions has lost the engine of the film.
items.check: Judge cites recap timestamps where the four-person family is visible together OR where the four individuals are shown in adjacent shots all inside the same cramped working-class home. Pass if four such individuals are clearly framed as one household.

items.criterion: A first-time viewer of the recap can identify that members of the poor family are intentionally getting hired into, or otherwise infiltrating, the wealthy family's household.
items.why: This is the single load-bearing narrative beat for the teaser. If the viewer cannot infer the con, the trailer has failed at its main job, selling the heist hook. Source calibration: golden builds this across 00:17-01:24 (Min-hyuk pitch → forged certificate → mansion arrival → Da-hye tutoring → Jessica jingle).
items.check: Judge writes one sentence describing what they think the film is about based only on the recap, then cites the specific recap timestamps that ground "members of the poor family are getting hired into / infiltrating the rich family's household." Pass only if those timestamps exist AND the written summary makes the infiltration explicit.

items.criterion: Without any on-screen explanatory text or narrator VO, the recap visually conveys a sharp contrast between a cramped low-income domestic space and an opulent modernist domestic space.
items.why: Class contrast is the visual grammar of the film and of the marketing. The contrast must be readable from visuals alone, title cards saying "rich vs poor" are not a substitute. The criterion is intentionally narrower than V-PARK-MANSION-SHOWN: this item asks whether the contrast is *legible*, not whether the spaces are individually present.
items.check: Judge confirms that (a) at least one cramped low-light low-ceiling interior shot is present, (b) at least one open/glass/lawn upscale-mansion shot is present, and (c) the contrast is established without any on-screen text reading "rich" / "poor" / "class" or equivalent explainer-style label. Pass only if all three hold.

items.criterion: The recap signals that the film's tone changes from comedy/heist to something darker, using at least one of: a critic pull-quote card whose visible text references mutation/twist/dark turn (e.g., "mutates into something else", "twisted", "nerve-wracking"); a sustained shift in shot palette to rain/dark interiors in the back half; a clear shift to a heavier orchestral cue in the back half.
items.why: A teaser that never hints at the shift is just a comedy trailer; a teaser that shows the shift is a spoiler trailer. The "imply, don't show" capability is the unique-difficulty axis. Source calibration: golden uses pull-quotes at 01:25-01:55 and a clear palette/score shift starting around 01:41.
items.check: Judge cites at least one recap timestamp matching one of the three signals: a pull-quote-style critic card with mutation/twist language, an extended rain/dark-interior block in the back half, or an audible score shift to heavier orchestration in the back half. Pass if any one of these signals is observed.

items.criterion: The final 10 seconds of the recap (excluding any silent billing-block tail card) do NOT resolve the film's plot: the viewer is not told who lives in the basement, no act of violence is shown, no ending dialogue line spells out the film's thesis.
items.why: A teaser must leave the central question intact. This is the curiosity-gap payoff. Item is phrased as a positive (the curiosity gap is present) but operates by checking that no resolution material has slipped into the final 10 seconds.
items.check: Judge cites the final 10 seconds of pre-billing runtime and confirms (a) no shot reveals a previously-unseen male character behind a door / from a hidden room, (b) no shot depicts one person injuring another, (c) no on-screen text or audible line states what the film "is really about." Pass only if all three hold.

items.criterion: The recap contains no on-screen text or audible line that (a) names a character with a name not used in the original film, or (b) makes a plot claim the film does not support (e.g., a card reading "the family who sold their daughter", "based on a true story", "the demon in the basement").
items.why: An agent VO failure mode is fabricating plot from the high-saliency footage it has access to; this item blocks invented premise even when the visuals are clean.
items.check: Judge transcribes every on-screen full-screen text card and every audible voiceover line (if any) and confirms none names a character or asserts a plot beat that is not directly supported by the visible footage of the recap. Pass only if no invented name or claim is found.

items.criterion: The recap shows the secret basement bunker beneath the Park house: a previously-hidden door behind a kitchen shelf, the dark concrete stairs leading down from the kitchen, the bunker interior itself, OR a male character of any age who emerges from such a hidden door or is seen inside such an underground room.
items.why: The bunker reveal is the single largest narrative twist in the film and the most rigorously withheld element of every official trailer. A single frame of it kills the genre-shift the entire trailer is built to protect. Source calibration: the hidden door / Geun-sae reveal sits at roughly 01:15:30-01:16:40 of the source.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of any shot showing (a) a hidden door behind kitchen shelving sliding/swinging open, (b) downward concrete stairs leading from a kitchen to a basement room, (c) an underground room with shelves, lamps, and a man living in it, or (d) a previously-unseen male character emerging from such a door or staircase. Penalty fires if any one such timestamp exists.

items.criterion: The recap shows physical violence between people during the outdoor garden birthday-party setting: a guest or family member being stabbed, attacked with a kitchen tool, hit on the head, or visibly bleeding on a sunlit lawn while a children's party setup (tent, balloons, table arrangement) is present.
items.why: The birthday-party violence at 01:56-02:04 of the source is the act that completes the genre shift; showing any of it destroys the marketing arc and makes the trailer a tragedy trailer rather than a teaser.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of any shot depicting an act of physical violence between people occurring in a clearly outdoor sunlit garden / party setting (visible tent, party table, lawn). Penalty fires if any one such timestamp exists.

items.criterion: The recap shows the film's final coda: a man living alone in a basement bunker writing a letter, a person blinking a domestic lamp/light on and off in a coded pattern as a deliberate communication, OR a "dream" montage of someone arriving at, buying, or moving into the Park mansion in the closing seconds.
items.why: The film's resolution lives in the coda at 02:04-02:12 of the source. A teaser ending on the resolution has switched subtypes from teaser to explainer.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of any shot matching one of (a) a solitary man in a confined basement-style room writing or composing, (b) a single domestic light being deliberately flicked on/off in a sustained coded rhythm, (c) a sentimental wish-fulfilment montage of arriving at or possessing the Park mansion. Penalty fires if any one such timestamp exists.

items.criterion: When characters' voices are heard in the recap, more than half the spoken lines are in Korean (whether subtitled or not), not dubbed English.
items.why: The film is a Korean-language production; dubbing destroys the festival-grade subtitled-foreign-language posture the brief asks for.
items.check: Judge counts the number of distinct spoken lines from on-screen characters and tallies how many are in Korean vs. any other language. Pass if Korean lines outnumber non-Korean lines.

items.criterion: An instrumental score (not a pop song with vocals) is audible across at least 70% of the recap's runtime.
items.why: Trailers for prestige films are score-driven, not needle-drop-driven; the Parasite score (Jung Jae-il) is part of the film's identity.
items.check: Judge identifies stretches of the recap where instrumental score is audible and computes the fraction of total runtime covered. Pass if that fraction is ≥ 0.70.

items.criterion: The score in the recap's first half is recognisably lighter (harpsichord, plucked strings, baroque chamber-style, faster tempo with mischievous lift) than the score in the recap's second half (heavier orchestral strings, denser texture, lower-register sustains, or dread/menace coloration).
items.why: The two-section music arc is the audio equivalent of the genre shift. A trailer with a single tonal mood across all 2 minutes has betrayed the central capability the rubric grades. Source calibration: golden moves from Belt-of-Faith harpsichord (~00:30-01:25) into thicker orchestral writing (~01:30+) and into pre-title silence + stinger hits (~02:00+).
items.check: Judge characterises the music in the first 45 seconds of the recap and in the final 45 seconds, then confirms the second half is recognisably heavier / denser / more dread-coloured than the first. Pass if the two halves are recognisably distinct in this direction.

items.criterion: Immediately before the full-screen "PARASITE" title card, there is a noticeable drop in audio energy, a silence of at least 0.4 seconds, or a sudden score cut to near-silence followed by a single percussive hit.
items.why: The pre-title silence is the trailer's most reliable sound-design beat; without it the title card lands without punctuation. Source calibration: golden has a ~2 second silence band at 02:14+ and the title at 02:07-02:14 is preceded by a brief score drop.
items.check: Judge cites the recap timestamp of the "PARASITE" title card and confirms that the 1.0 second of audio immediately before it contains at least 0.4 seconds of near-silence or a hard score cut, NOT a continuous music wash. Pass if the pre-title drop is present.

items.criterion: The recap's audio has no audible dropouts of 0.5 seconds or longer in the middle of a spoken line, no hard clipped / over-driven bursts, and no sudden mid-line music cuts that chop a dialogue line in half.
items.why: Trailer-grade polish; rough audio breakpoints are the most common AI-edit tell.
items.check: Judge listens through the recap and confirms (a) no mid-line dialogue dropout ≥ 0.5s, (b) no clipped bursts, (c) no music cut that severs an in-progress dialogue line. Pass only if all three hold.

items.criterion: The recap contains no voiceover line that was not spoken on-screen by a visible character in the film, regardless of language. (Excludes critic pull-quote text presented purely visually.)
items.why: Added narrator audio is one of the easiest ways for an agent to fake "recap legibility" and breaks the source-audio convention. This item bans any off-screen narrator track, including plot-describing narration.
items.check: Judge identifies any audible voice that is not visibly attributable to an on-screen character at the time it is heard. If any such off-screen voice is identifiable, the item fails. Pass only if all audible voices are on-screen at the moment they speak.

items.criterion: The recap contains no commercial pop song with vocals, no licensed needle-drop track, and no music cue that audibly diverges from the orchestral/chamber score of the film.
items.why: Replacing the score with a pop cue is a recognised low-effort agent failure; it also dates the trailer instantly and signals the agent did not respect the audio brief.
items.check: Judge listens for any non-instrumental music or commercial-pop cue and confirms none is present. Pass only if no such cue is found.

items.criterion: VIOLATION STATE: at least one second of audible Korean speech plays in the recap WITHOUT a readable English subtitle in the safe area. The bad state is "Korean dialogue heard, no English text on screen to read." Return pass=true (fire the penalty) if you observe this violation state for >= 1.0 cumulative seconds.
items.why: This is a North American theatrical trailer for a Korean-language film. A US theatrical audience cannot follow Korean dialogue without subtitles; a trailer that strips them defeats the deliverable's core purpose. The brief explicitly notes "Keep the subtitles in the safe area; this audience will be reading."
items.check: Identify every Korean-dialogue moment in the recap. For each, check whether a legible English subtitle is visible in the safe area during the spoken line. Sum the cumulative duration where Korean is audible AND no English subtitle is visible. Return pass=true (fire) iff that sum is >= 1.0 seconds.

items.criterion: VIOLATION STATE: the recap has stripped the Korean source-actor dialogue. The bad state is "less than 4 cumulative seconds of audible Korean speech from source actors across the entire recap" — an English-VO-only or music-only edit that has erased the language identity of a Korean film. Return pass=true (fire the penalty) if you observe this violation state.
items.why: Brief commissions Korean dialogue as the trailer's voice ("Korean dialogue with subtitles is the voice of this trailer"). A recap that strips all Korean dialogue, or replaces it with an English narrator, has lost the language identity of the film and defeats the brief's "this audience will be reading" framing.
items.check: Identify every timestamp where Korean speech from source actors is clearly audible (not buried, not at -70dB under VO). Sum the cumulative duration of clearly audible Korean speech. Return pass=true (fire) iff cumulative clearly-audible Korean is < 4.0 seconds.

items.criterion: Within the first 60 seconds of the recap, at least one of the four Bong-comedy register signals is present: (1) a playful or baroque-light score cue, (2) a rhythmic comic-coded dialogue beat (rehearsed self-introduction, fake credential reveal), (3) a stylised heist set-piece shot (slow-motion peach-fuzz, document forgery close-up, family lounging stylishly in a wealthier home), or (4) a visibly comedic shot composition such as a deadpan reaction or absurd staging.
items.why: The genre-shift the trailer is built around only works if the first half is comedic enough to be subverted by the second half. Rewarding the presence of at least one comedy/heist signal in the first 60 seconds tests the Bong-comedy register without penalising trailers that lean thriller-leaning by craft choice.
items.check: Judge characterises the tone of the first 60 seconds of the recap and confirms whether ANY of the four comedy/heist signals are present: (1) playful or baroque-light score in the first half, (2) a rhythmic comic-coded dialogue beat, (3) a stylised heist set-piece shot (slow-motion fuzz, document forgery close-up, family lounging stylishly in a wealthier home), (4) a visibly comedic shot composition such as a deadpan reaction or absurd staging. Pass if at least one signal is observed.
